entries.name: Beam decoding with a monotone-score stopping certificate
entries.definition: A layer-based sequence beam decoder that retains the best completed hypothesis seen so far and stops when the highest current prefix score cannot exceed that incumbent under a score that never increases with extension.
entries.identity_notes: This is Huang, Zhao and Ma’s 2017 optimal-ending procedure, with optimality explicitly limited by the retained beam. It differs from stopping on a completed top-ranked item without remembering earlier completions, from counting completed outputs, and from score-prioritized best-first expansion with per-length budgets.
entries.mechanism: Expand the current beam by one token and retain the highest-scoring candidates under a fixed beam policy. Do not extend EOS-complete hypotheses. Maintain the best completed hypothesis encountered in retained beams. Once that incumbent exists, stop when the maximum current prefix score is at most its score. Products of conditional probabilities in [0,1], or their cumulative log probabilities, cannot increase with extension, so descendants of retained active prefixes cannot improve the incumbent when the inequality holds.
entries.locator: Sections 2–3, Equations (1)–(2), Theorems 1–2, printed p. 2135 / PDF p. 2
limitations: The certificate concerns descendants of retained beam prefixes. It does not recover prefixes pruned by finite width or guarantee global MAP decoding.
A non-increasing extension score and a stored completed incumbent are required. Length normalization or positive rewards can invalidate the raw-prefix bound and need a different certificate.
The paper compares stopping times under the same beam evolution and a specific historical top-completed baseline. It does not establish universally fastest decoding or current software defaults.
Better model score does not imply better translation quality; the source reports short-output problems under pure probability scoring.
Finite resource limits, absent EOS completions, empty beams and tie conventions need explicit implementation policies. No unconditional finite-time termination claim is made.

entries.name: Bounded length reward for sequence scoring
entries.definition: A sequence scoring rule that adds a fixed nonnegative reward per generated position up to a finite length cap, giving score S(y)+r·min(l,|y|) instead of rewarding every additional position without bound.
entries.identity_notes: The cap limits how much reward can accumulate; it is not itself a maximum allowed output length. This is the bounded reward in Huang et al. 2017, called bounded word-reward by Yang et al. 2018. It differs from division by output length, an uncapped word reward and a reward rate recomputed from beam statistics.
entries.mechanism: Add r·min(l,n) to cumulative log probability S(y), where n is the hypothesis length and r≥0. The 2017 method estimates l from a development-set target/source length ratio times the input length. For a current prefix at depth i, all remaining reward is bounded by r·max(l−i,0). Its total completion-score bound simplifies to S(prefix)+r·l. A beam decoder may stop once the maximum such active-prefix bound is no greater than the best completed adjusted score.
entries.locator: Section 4, score definition and Equations (3)–(4), printed pp. 2136–2137 / PDF pp. 3–4
limitations: The score is a decoding preference, not a probability distribution or an intrinsic translation-quality measure.
The reward rate and length-cap estimate require specification. A development-set average length ratio need not transfer to every sentence or domain.
The stopping bound assumes non-increasing log probability, nonnegative fixed reward and a fixed finite cap for the input; its beam-relative guarantee does not undo finite-width pruning.
Reward saturation does not prohibit outputs longer than the cap. Tokenization, length counting and EOS handling must be specified in an implementation.
No numerical BLEU improvement, universal quality advantage or current implementation behavior is asserted.

entries.name: Bounded word reward with predicted length
entries.definition: A sequence rescoring method that adds a fixed word reward only up to an input-specific length predicted from encoder states, replacing a corpus-level generation-ratio cap with Lpred(x).
entries.identity_notes: This is Yang et al.’s predicted-length bounded word-reward variant. It changes the cap, while retaining a separately tuned reward rate r. It is not the beam-statistic adaptive reward or the brevity-penalty normalized score, and it is not a standalone trained length-predictor instance.
entries.mechanism: Feed the mean source encoder hidden state to a two-layer multilayer perceptron to predict a target/source generation ratio, then multiply it by the source length to obtain Lpred(x). Score candidate y by S(x,y)+r·min(|y|,Lpred(x)), where S is cumulative log probability. The predictor is evaluated from the input and the reward cap is fixed for that input during decoding.
entries.locator: Sections 4.2–4.2.1, Equations (8)–(9), printed p. 3056 / PDF p. 3
limitations: The method still requires a learned length predictor and a tuned reward rate; replacing the corpus ratio does not make the complete system parameter-free.
Predicted length is a reward cap, not automatically an enforced maximum sequence length or an accurate target for every input.

A usable nonnegative length prediction, tokenizer conventions and integration with the decoder must be specified. The paper passage does not provide a complete predictor training or calibration protocol.
Finite beam width still prunes hypotheses. Neither accurate length prediction nor a stopping certificate implies globally optimal output or universally better translation quality.
The empirical source scope is Chinese-to-English news translation; no numerical result is curated.

entries.name: Bounded adaptive reward for sequence scoring
entries.definition: A beam-dependent sequence rescoring rule that adds per-step rewards derived from the beam’s mean negative log token probability, accumulating them only up to a predicted output-length cap.
entries.identity_notes: Yang et al.’s bounded adaptive-reward changes the reward rate with the decoding step, unlike fixed-r bounded word-reward. It is a beam-conditioned scoring method rather than a reinforcement-learning reward-training algorithm or a beam-independent probability model.
entries.mechanism: For a b-item beam at step t, compute r_t=−(1/b)·sum_i log p(word_i), using the last generated token probability of each beam item in its own context. Add accumulated r_t values to the sequence log probability up to the smaller of the candidate length and predicted length. After the cap is passed, no additional reward accrues, so the adjusted score cannot increase with further nonpositive log-probability increments. The source then permits stopping when the best current adjusted score is below the best completed adjusted score.
entries.locator: Section 4.2.2, Equations (10)–(11), and Section 5.2 final paragraph, printed pp. 3056–3057 / PDF pp. 3–4
limitations: The reward sequence depends on the beam and model probabilities. Changing beam policy can change the score assigned to a completed hypothesis.
Removing a manually tuned constant reward rate does not remove the trained translation model, length predictor, beam size or other implementation choices.

The printed sum uses a predicted length as its upper limit without specifying a noninteger rounding policy. A discrete implementation must define the effective integer cap and EOS/token counting; the record does not assert an author-approved rounding convention.
Equation (10) assumes b available beam entries and defined token log probabilities. Empty or shrunken beams and zero-probability tokens require an explicit policy.

The stated stopping argument applies after reward saturation with a completed incumbent. It is limited to retained beam continuations, not global sequence optimality or guaranteed quality improvement.

entries.name: Brevity-penalty normalization for sequence scoring
entries.definition: A sequence rescoring rule that adds a predicted-length brevity penalty in log space to average token log probability: S(x,y)/|y| + min(1−Lpred(x)/|y|,0).
entries.identity_notes: BP-Norm is Yang et al.’s predicted-length decoding score. It resembles the algebraic structure of BLEU’s brevity penalty but does not compute n-gram precision, use an actual reference translation at inference, or equal the BLEU evaluation metric. It differs from plain average log probability and additive word rewards.
entries.mechanism: Predict a target length from the input using the paper’s encoder-state length predictor. For a nonempty hypothesis of length n, combine average log probability S/n with log brevity penalty min(1−Lpred/n,0). For decoding with a genuine finite maximum output length R, a current raw log score S_t≤0 yields an upper bound S_t/R on descendant BP-Norm scores. Compare the maximum active-prefix bound with the best completed BP-Norm score before stopping.
entries.locator: Section 4.2.3 Equation (12), transformed score and Section 5.2 Equation (13), printed pp. 3056–3057 / PDF pp. 3–4
limitations: Lpred is a prediction, not a reference length or a proven upper bound on output length. The S_t/R stopping bound requires that admissible completions actually have length at most R.

The experiments set R to the predicted length. This supports the stopping guarantee only under an enforced length cap or another justification that all allowed completions obey that bound; a forecast alone is insufficient.
The formula requires nonempty hypotheses and a valid length prediction. A BOS-only prefix needs separate handling; length and EOS conventions must be specified.
The score is neither a normalized probability nor BLEU itself. Improved search score does not imply better human translation quality.

The source’s hyperparameter-free comparison concerns removal of a separately tuned reward constant, not absence of trained models, a length predictor or decoding choices. Finite beam pruning remains approximate.

entries.name: Absolute threshold pruning for sequence beams
entries.definition: A sequence-beam pruning procedure that first applies the beam-size cap, then discards candidates whose score is at least a specified positive margin below the best score in that capped candidate list.
entries.identity_notes: This is Freitag and Al-Onaizan’s absolute threshold pruning rule. It uses an additive score difference, unlike their relative-score and last-token relative thresholds. It is an additional local pruning step, not a stopping certificate or a method that automatically widens the beam.
entries.mechanism: First retain candidates up to the current beam width. Let M be the maximum score in that candidate list and let a>0 be the absolute pruning margin. Discard a candidate when its score is at most M−a, including equality as printed in Equation (2). Continue decoding with the survivors; applying pruning after the cap can reduce the active count without refilling from previously discarded candidates.
entries.locator: Section 4, introductory paragraph and Absolute Threshold Pruning, Equation (2), printed p. 57 / PDF p. 2

entries.name: Maximum candidates per node in sequence beam pruning
entries.definition: A sequence-beam pruning procedure that limits how many retained candidate extensions may come from the same predecessor hypothesis, discarding a candidate when the allowed number of better-scoring siblings is already retained.
entries.identity_notes: This is the Maximum Candidates per Node rule of Freitag and Al-Onaizan. Same history means the common predecessor prefix, not arbitrary semantic similarity between full sequences. It differs from an additive diversity penalty, grouping beams into separate searches or imposing a global frontier capacity.
entries.mechanism: Apply the current beam-size cap, then keep at most m candidate continuations for each predecessor prefix by score. A candidate is discarded once m better-scoring candidates with that same predecessor are in the retained list. This is extra pruning after the initial top-beam selection; it does not specify refilling with candidates outside that initial list.
entries.locator: Section 4, introductory paragraph and Maximum Candidates per Node, printed p. 57 / PDF p. 2
limitations: A positive integer per-parent cap and deterministic tie handling must be specified. The source’s prose refers to better-scoring candidates without a complete tie policy.
Limiting sibling extensions can remove the prefix of the best eventual sequence; this is not an exact or complete search guarantee.
More varied parent prefixes do not guarantee semantic diversity or improved translation quality. The paper’s conclusion reports no translation-quality improvement from this diversity intervention.
The inherited decoder determines EOS processing, generation length and changing active-beam width. The pruning rule alone is not a complete decoder implementation.
No specific current library implementation, numeric quality gain or universal runtime benefit is asserted.

source_analysis.caveat: All six text pages were read. Raw probability/log-probability stopping is distinct from bounded positive reward. Reward saturation is not an output-length prohibition. No numerical comparison is curated.

The adaptive sum lacks an explicit noninteger-cap convention. The BP-Norm bound is asserted only with a genuine maximum length; a prediction by itself is insufficient.

All five text pages were read. The method first caps candidates, then prunes. Equation (2) includes equality. curator_analysis.claim_tested: How score coordinates and a true maximum output length affect pruning/stopping statements.
curator_analysis.observation: For negative log scores -1,-2,-3 and ratio 0.6, literal multiplicative log pruning retains nothing, while probability-ratio pruning retains the best item. A BP-Norm completion longer than a predicted R can beat an incumbent after the prediction-based inequality would stop.
